title: PDI Machine Learning Specialty Exam
description: 20 questions drawn from a pool of 41, covering machine-learning concepts and the PDI credit-card fraud workflow: the R setup, choosing a model with AutoML, and training and scoring a GBM in R. Pass mark is 80%. Open-book — browse any page, hover glossary terms, or ask the AI assistant. Your answers are saved as you go. Explanations appear after submission.

questions.scenario: A fraud team holds years of transactions already marked fraud or legitimate. It also wants to catch kinds of fraud nobody has seen before.
questions.prompt: Which learning approaches fit the two aims?
options: Supervised for the known patterns, unsupervised for new kinds
Unsupervised for the known patterns, supervised for new kinds
Supervised for both, as the marked history covers new kinds too
Unsupervised for both, as labels only bias the model's judgement
questions.explanation: Supervised learning learns patterns from historical fraud cases, which the marked history supplies; unsupervised methods are for identifying new, previously unseen types of fraud, which no label describes yet. Swapping them asks labels to describe what has never been labelled. The history cannot mark fraud no one has seen. The labels are what make the known-pattern model possible, not a bias to avoid.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Overview

questions.scenario: Customer details sit in a relational database and orders in another table. Which orders proved fraudulent is recorded only in a historical fraud report kept as a CSV.
questions.prompt: What does that CSV contribute to a supervised fraud model?
options: Extra features, describing each customer's billing address
The label, marking which past orders turned out to be fraud
Nothing, since the model infers fraud from the orders alone
A finished model, ready to score each incoming order
questions.explanation: Supervised learning learns from historical fraud cases, so the report's record of which orders were fraud becomes the target the preparation joins onto the orders. Without it there is nothing to learn the outcome from. Billing details come from the customer tables, not the fraud report. A CSV of past fraud is data, not a model.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: A gbm model is trained with n.trees = 500. Its out-of-bag error falls until about 300 trees, then creeps up again to 500.
questions.prompt: What does scoring with all 500 trees risk?
options: A slower model, but one that is otherwise just as good
Underfitting, as 500 trees are too few for the data
Overfitting, which is why gbm.perf picks the tree count
Nothing, as each extra tree can only improve the model
questions.explanation: gbm.perf with the OOB method returns the tree count where out-of-bag error is lowest; using more trees than that would overfit, and fewer would underfit, so scoring uses best_trees. Too few trees is underfitting, the opposite of this curve. A rising error shows extra trees can make things worse. The cost is accuracy on new data, not only speed.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The training script fits reported_as_fraud_historic ~ . on the frame it receives. A transaction_id column, unique to every row, was left in that frame.
questions.prompt: What happens to transaction_id?
options: It is used as a predictor, though it describes nothing
It is used only to join the predictions back afterwards
It is used as the target, since it is the frame's key
It is skipped, as gbm ignores columns with unique values
questions.explanation: The formula's ~ . means predict the target from every other column in the frame, so an identifier left there becomes a predictor even though it describes nothing about the transaction and can only be memorised. gbm does not drop columns for being unique. The target is named on the left of the ~. Joining back is done later with cbind in the prediction script, not by the training formula.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The training script converts reported_as_fraud_historic with as.numeric(as.factor(x)) - 1 before calling gbm.
questions.prompt: Why is 1 subtracted?
options: To shift each fraud probability below the 0.5 threshold
To exclude the first transaction from the training data
as.factor numbering starts at 1, so it yields 0 and 1
To turn the target into a continuous dollar amount
questions.explanation: as.factor creates levels and as.numeric numbers them 1 and 2, so subtracting 1 gives 0 for not fraud and 1 for fraud, the binary target the bernoulli distribution expects. No row is dropped; the arithmetic applies to every value. The threshold is applied to predictions at scoring time, not to the training target. The target is binary, not an amount.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: A fraud model was trained last week. Today's transactions have arrived and need fraud probabilities.
questions.prompt: What does scoring them involve?
options: Retraining on today's rows before anything is predicted
Recomputing the model's accuracy against today's rows
Rerunning the AutoML search to pick a fresh model first
Loading the saved model and predicting, with no retraining
questions.explanation: The prediction transformation loads gbm_fraud.rdata, saved by training, and calls predict on the new rows, so scoring needs no training at all. Retraining is a separate job. AutoML was used once to choose the algorithm. Accuracy cannot be computed on new rows whose outcome is not yet known.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: A developer adds cv.folds = 5 to the gbm call inside the R Script Executor. The transformation then aborts the whole JVM.
questions.prompt: Why does it abort?
options: Its extra processes exceed select()'s FD_SETSIZE limit
Five folds use more memory than the R step can be given
Cross-validation needs more trees than n.trees allows
gbm cannot run cross-validation on a binary target
questions.explanation: JRI runs R inside the JVM process, and cross-validation spawns extra processes that exceed the FD_SETSIZE limit of 1024 in Linux's select() call, so the JVM aborts; that is why the script uses OOB estimation instead. The tree count is unrelated to folds. Memory is not the reason given. The failure comes from where R runs, not from the target type.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: To keep the artifact small, someone changes the training script to save only gbm_model to gbm_fraud.rdata.
questions.prompt: What breaks in the prediction script?
options: predict is passed n.trees = best_trees, which no longer loads
Nothing, as predict always uses all 500 trees by default
The bernoulli distribution is lost, so outputs turn to counts
load() fails, as an .rdata file must hold two objects
questions.explanation: The prediction script loads the file and calls predict with n.trees = best_trees, the OOB-chosen tree count saved alongside the model, so without it that object is missing. The script names best_trees explicitly rather than relying on a default. An .rdata file can hold one object or many. The distribution is part of gbm_model, which is still saved.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: R is installed and works in a terminal. PDI must now run an R Script Executor step.
questions.prompt: Why is rJava needed as well?
options: It bridges Java and R, so Java-based PDI can call into R
It is needed only when an R script draws a chart
It installs R itself, since the base R install is not enough
It converts R scripts to Java before PDI runs them
questions.explanation: rJava (with its JRI library) is what lets a Java application such as PDI run R, which is why the R steps need it. It does not install R; R is installed separately. Scripts run as R, not translated to Java. Every R step needs the bridge, not only charting ones.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Prerequisite Tasks

questions.scenario: Java was upgraded on a machine where rJava used to build, and rJava now fails to build.
questions.prompt: What does sudo R CMD javareconf do about it?
options: Disables the Java bridge so that R runs without it
Reinstalls Java at the version R was first set up with
Detects current Java and updates R's config to match
Downgrades rJava to match the previous version of Java
questions.explanation: R CMD javareconf detects the Java installation now on the system and updates R's configuration files to match, so rJava builds against it. It installs nothing and downgrades nothing. Disabling the bridge would defeat the purpose, since PDI's R steps depend on it.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Prerequisite Tasks

questions.scenario: rJava has been built and verified with library(rJava); .jinit(), but Spoon still cannot load R support for an R Script Executor step.
questions.prompt: Which file has to be copied into Spoon's native-lib directory?
options: libR.so, from R's own lib folder
libjvm.so, from the JDK's server folder
libjri.so, from rJava's jri folder
rJava.so, from rJava's libs folder
questions.explanation: libjri.so, from the rJava package's jri folder, goes into Spoon's native-lib/linux/x86_64 directory (owned by the PDI user) so PDI can load the R-Java interface. libR.so is R's own library, which R finds through R_HOME. rJava.so is the R-side package library, not what Spoon loads. libjvm.so is Java's, which Spoon already runs on.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Prerequisite Tasks

questions.scenario: The AutoML model search needs Python with H2O and other ML libraries, and nobody wants to depend on what happens to be installed on each workstation.
questions.prompt: What does Google Colab provide here?
options: A hosted database to hold the scored transactions
A managed PDI server that runs the transformations for you
Browser-based Jupyter, with ML runtimes ready-made
An R environment, so the R steps can run remotely
questions.explanation: Colab runs Jupyter notebooks in the browser with preconfigured runtimes for common ML libraries, so the search runs on the uploaded H2O.csv without local setup. It does not run PDI transformations. Scored results are written by PDI, not stored in Colab. The R steps run inside PDI through rJava, not in Colab.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Prerequisite Tasks

questions.scenario: R and rJava are installed and libjri.so has been copied into Spoon's native-lib directory, but the R Script Executor step still fails.
questions.prompt: Which two remaining steps are most likely missing?
options: Restarting so the newly copied libraries are registered
Removing the default JDK that rJava was built against
Installing h2o and py4j in the Python virtual environment
Uploading H2O.csv to the Colab notebook first
Setting R_HOME and R_LIBS_USER, with R's bin on PATH
questions.explanation: PDI's R integration needs the environment variables, R_HOME and R_LIBS_USER in /etc/environment with R's bin directory on PATH, and a restart may be needed to register the libraries. The Python venv serves the H2O work, not the R steps. Colab is for the AutoML search. Removing the JDK would break the rJava build it depends on.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Prerequisite Tasks

questions.scenario: The gbm package was installed by running R as the developer's own user. When PDI runs the training step as a different service user, R reports there is no package called gbm.
questions.prompt: What explains the failure, and the fix?
options: gbm went into that user's library; install it with sudo -i R
rJava is missing gbm; rebuild rJava with --with-java-home
gbm cannot run inside PDI; train the model in Colab instead
The package name is case-sensitive; call library(GBM)
questions.explanation: Running R without sudo installs packages for that user only, so another user cannot load them; sudo -i R installs them system-wide. gbm is exactly what the PDI training step uses. rJava is the Java bridge; it does not carry R packages. R package names are case-sensitive, and the package is gbm in lower case.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Prerequisite Tasks

questions.scenario: Before building the fraud pipeline, a developer wants proof that the R Script Executor step is wired to a working R.
questions.prompt: What is the quickest check?
options: Open the step and confirm that the R home field is filled in
Run the full training transformation to see if it finishes
Check that the installed R version matches the documented one
Run library(datasets); iris and use Test Script to see the rows
questions.explanation: A two-line script that returns the built-in iris data, previewed with Test Script, exercises the whole chain from PDI through rJava to R. The full training run takes far longer and mixes in other failures. A matching version number does not prove the bridge works. A filled-in field looks right without showing anything runs.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Prerequisite Tasks

questions.scenario: A team has a labelled fraud dataset and no strong view on which algorithm suits it.
questions.prompt: What does H2O AutoML do for them?
options: Deploys the winning model straight into the PDI pipeline
Trains one model that needs no further evaluation at all
Shortlists strong models without lengthy manual tuning
Removes the need for a labelled target column in the data
questions.explanation: AutoML automatically discovers well-performing models, giving a shortlist of candidates to compare on the right metric. Its output still has to be judged, which is what the metrics cheat sheet is for. The fraud search runs on the labelled dataset. Deployment is a separate step: the H2O result pointed to GBM, which is then trained in R inside PDI.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Overview

questions.scenario: AutoML has produced a leaderboard of fraud classifiers on data where fraud is about 1% of rows.
questions.prompt: Which metric should rank the candidates?
options: AUC
Accuracy
RMSE
AUCPR
questions.explanation: AUCPR is the best single-number metric for imbalanced classification and is used to compare candidates before tuning thresholds. AUC is a sanity check on ranking that can look good while precision is poor. Accuracy is the trap on 1% fraud. RMSE is a regression-style error on probabilities, not decision-friendly here.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: Genuine fraud is about 1% of transactions. A colleague proposes judging models by plain accuracy, since it is the one number the business already understands.
questions.prompt: What is the fairest assessment of the proposal?
options: Reject it: a do-nothing model would score 99% here
Reject it, and rank the candidates on RMSE in its place
Accept it, provided RMSE is reported alongside accuracy
Accept it: accuracy is computed alike for every candidate
questions.explanation: With fraud at 1%, predicting legitimate for every row is 99% accurate and useless, which is why accuracy is a trap here. Being computed the same way for every model does not make it meaningful. RMSE is a regression-style error on probabilities, so adding it or ranking on it does not judge the fraud decision.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: A fraud model reports an AUC of 0.97, and the team wants to put it into production on that figure alone.
questions.prompt: What is the problem with that?
options: AUC cannot be computed on imbalanced data, so 0.97 is meaningless
AUC rates ranking; precision at the threshold used may be poor
Nothing at all, since any AUC above 0.95 is enough on its own
AUC applies only to regression problems, never to classification
questions.explanation: AUC measures how well the model ranks fraud above legitimate transactions and can look good even when precision is poor at useful thresholds, so it is a sanity check rather than the decision. It can be computed on imbalanced data; it just says less there. It is a classification metric. No AUC figure settles behaviour at the threshold you run.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: A fraud model raises 100 alerts in a month, and 20 of them are real fraud. There were 50 fraudulent transactions in total that month.
questions.prompt: What are its precision and recall?
options: Precision 50% and recall 40%
Precision 40% and recall 20%
Precision 20% and recall 40%
Precision 20% and recall 80%
questions.explanation: Precision is how many alerts are real fraud, 20 of 100, so 20%; recall is how much of the fraud is caught, 20 of 50, so 40%. Swapping them confuses alerts with frauds. 80% would mean 40 frauds caught. 50% treats the total fraud count as the alert count.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: For one card issuer every undetected fraud is refunded at the bank's expense, while a false alarm only means a customer confirming a purchase. Two colleagues disagree on whether to prioritise precision or recall.
questions.prompt: Which position is better supported?
options: Precision, as false alarms are the only cost the bank controls
Recall, and precision then stops carrying any information at all
Neither, as accuracy balances the two and should be used instead
Recall, as missed fraud costs more, within the alert volume
questions.explanation: When fraud losses are expensive the guidance is to prioritise recall, and here missed fraud is the costly error; precision still sets how many alerts the team must work through. The bank controls both errors through the threshold. Accuracy is the trap on imbalanced data. Precision remains informative even when recall leads, because it measures the alert burden.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: A team has twelve candidate fraud models from AutoML and must also settle the probability at which an alert is raised.
questions.prompt: In what order should those decisions be made?
options: Choose the model with the lowest RMSE, then leave the threshold at 0.5
Compare candidates on AUCPR, then tune the chosen one's threshold
Tune a threshold for each of the twelve, then compare them on AUC
Set one threshold first, then choose the model with best accuracy
questions.explanation: AUCPR compares candidates before thresholds are tuned, and the threshold is then set for the chosen model to balance precision and recall. Accuracy is the wrong yardstick on imbalanced data. AUC is a sanity check, not the comparison metric. RMSE is not decision-friendly, and 0.5 is a default to adjust, not a decision.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: The data preparation is done in PDI, and the AutoML search runs in a Colab notebook.
questions.prompt: What passes from one to the other?
options: The H2O.csv file that autoML.ktr writes, uploaded to Colab
Nothing, as Colab queries PDI's database connections live
The autoML.ktr transformation itself, which Colab runs
A trained model artifact that Colab goes on to refine
questions.explanation: Running autoML.ktr in PDI creates data/H2O.csv, which is uploaded to Colab when prompted; the handover is a file. Colab runs notebooks, not PDI transformations. The model is trained in Colab, not received from PDI. Colab has no live connection to PDI's databases.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: The AutoML results in Colab point to a Gradient Boosting model as the best fit for the fraud data.
questions.prompt: How is that result carried into the PDI fraud workflow?
options: PDI calls Colab to score each new transaction
A GBM is trained in R inside PDI, on the same dataset
The leaderboard's CSV is loaded as if it were the model
The H2O model is copied unchanged into the R step
questions.explanation: The H2O results point to GBM, and the PDI workflow operationalises that choice by training a GBM with the R gbm package on the same dataset, saving the artifact and scoring with it. The H2O model itself is not moved into R. Scoring runs in PDI's R step, not in Colab. A leaderboard lists candidates; it is not a model.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: A fraud classifier leaderboard has been sorted by RMSE, and the top model by that measure is being put forward for deployment.
questions.prompt: Why is RMSE the wrong sort key here?
options: It is valid only on balanced data, so it would suit a higher fraud rate
It cannot be computed for classifiers, so the column is meaningless
It measures error on probabilities, not the quality of the fraud decision
It is right for ranking, but must be weighed against training time
questions.explanation: RMSE and MSE are regression-style errors on probabilities and are not decision-friendly for fraud, so they are mostly ignored; AUCPR ranks candidates. The column can be computed, which is why it appears. Balance is not the issue; it measures the wrong thing either way. Training time does not repair a metric that does not judge the decision.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: AutoML

questions.scenario: A colleague reviewing the gbm training script asks which values are chosen before training rather than produced by it.
questions.prompt: Which two are set before the model is trained?
options: n.trees = 500
best_trees (gbm.perf)
fraud_probability
OOB error per tree
shrinkage = 0.01
questions.explanation: n.trees, the number of boosting iterations, and shrinkage, the learning rate, are arguments passed to gbm before it runs. best_trees is computed from the trained model by gbm.perf. fraud_probability comes from predict at scoring time. The OOB error is measured during training, not chosen beforehand.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The gbm call in the training script sets bag.fraction = 0.5.
questions.prompt: What does that setting do?
options: Keeps half the rows back as a fixed test set
Fits each tree on a random half of the rows
Halves the learning rate on every iteration
Discards half the trees once training ends
questions.explanation: bag.fraction = 0.5 uses 50% of the data for each tree, which makes it a stochastic GBM; the rows left out of each tree are what out-of-bag estimation measures. No trees are discarded; gbm.perf only chooses how many to use. The sample is drawn afresh for each tree, not a fixed test set. The learning rate is shrinkage, set separately.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The training script sets distribution = "bernoulli" for a target holding 0 for not fraud and 1 for fraud.
questions.prompt: Why bernoulli?
options: The target is a continuous amount
The target has more than two classes
It makes the training run faster
The target is binary, fraud or not
questions.explanation: bernoulli is the distribution for binary classification, fraud yes or no, which is what the converted target holds. A continuous amount would call for a regression distribution. There are exactly two classes. The choice follows the target's type, not speed.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: Each tree in the fraud model may be at most four levels deep, and no terminal node may hold fewer than 10 observations.
questions.prompt: Which gbm settings express those limits?
options: shrinkage = 4, n.trees = 10
interaction.depth = 4, n.minobsinnode = 10
interaction.depth = 10, n.minobsinnode = 4
n.trees = 4, bag.fraction = 10
questions.explanation: interaction.depth sets the maximum depth of each tree and n.minobsinnode the minimum observations per terminal node. n.trees counts boosting iterations and bag.fraction is a share of rows between 0 and 1. shrinkage is the learning rate. The last option swaps the two values.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: A training script ends with the save() call that writes gbm_fraud.rdata, and the R Script Executor step then reports an error although the file was written.
questions.prompt: What should the script end with?
options: A print() of the saved model's full summary
A call to quit() so that the R session closes
The path of the .rdata file as a plain string
A data frame, such as one holding Finished
questions.explanation: The R Script Executor expects a data frame as the script's output, so the training script builds ok.df from a status value and returns it. Printed output is not the step's result. Quitting R would end the session PDI runs it in. A bare string is not a data frame.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The prediction script calls predict(gbm_model, newdata = test.df, n.trees = best_trees, type = "response").
questions.prompt: What does it return for each transaction?
options: A count of the trees that voted fraud
A fraud probability between 0 and 1
A 0 or 1 label from the 0.5 cut-off
The row's rank among all transactions
questions.explanation: With a bernoulli model, type = "response" returns probabilities on the 0 to 1 scale, with values closer to 1 more likely fraud. Boosted trees are summed into one score, not counted as votes. The 0/1 flag is made afterwards with ifelse(fraud_prob >= 0.5, 1, 0). The output is a probability per row, not a rank.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The business would rather review a few more legitimate transactions than let fraud through, and asks for the prediction script's cut-off to move from 0.5 to 0.3.
questions.prompt: What is the fairest assessment of the change?
options: It catches more fraud, at the cost of more false alarms
It changes only how the probability is displayed
It catches more fraud with no increase in false alarms
It has no effect until the model has been retrained
questions.explanation: Lowering the threshold flags transactions on weaker evidence, so more fraud is caught and more legitimate transactions are flagged; it is right only if reviewers can absorb the extra volume. False alarms do rise. The threshold decides predicted_fraud, so it changes which rows are flagged. It is applied to probabilities the model already produces, so no retraining is involved.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The training step fails because R cannot open a file whose path begins with the literal text ${Internal.Transformation.Filename.Directory}.
questions.prompt: What fixes it?
options: Escaping the dollar sign so R treats it as an R variable
Replacing the variable with the developer's own absolute path
Defining the variable in kettle.properties so R can read it
Enabling variable substitution on the R Script Executor step
questions.explanation: The path is resolved by PDI, so the step must substitute variables before handing the script to R; otherwise R receives the literal text. An absolute path breaks the folder-relative handoff when the files move. The variable is PDI's internal one, and R does not read kettle.properties. R has no such variable to refer to.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: Reviewers need each scored transaction's original fields beside its fraud probability and flag.
questions.prompt: What in the prediction script provides that?
options: load(), which restores the original rows with the model
cbind(test.df, pred.df), joining inputs to predictions
predict(), which returns the input fields with each score
as.data.frame(test), which adds the predictions to the rows
questions.explanation: The script binds the input frame and the predictions column-wise, so every input field travels downstream with fraud_probability, fraud_pct and predicted_fraud. load() restores the model and best_trees, not rows. predict returns probabilities only. as.data.frame(test) converts the incoming rows before scoring.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: Training and scoring are built as two transformations sequenced by a job, rather than as one transformation that trains and then predicts.
questions.prompt: What does that split make possible?
options: Staying under a limit on steps per transformation
Running R twice, which one transformation cannot do
Setting variables, which only a job is able to do
Each runs alone; the saved model is the handoff
questions.explanation: Training saves gbm_fraud.rdata and prediction loads it, so the two can run, be tested and be rerun independently, with the artifact as the seam. A transformation can hold several R steps. There is no step limit that forces the split. Transformations have parameters and variables of their own.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The training model must be fitted on every row of the prepared data in a single run of the R script.
questions.prompt: Which R Script Executor setting ensures that?
options: R frame name set to all, naming the data frame
Row handling, Number of rows to process, set to All
Variable substitution, so ${ALL} expands to the rows
Input frames set to every step in the transformation
questions.explanation: Row handling's Number of rows to process set to All passes every row to the script at once, so one model is fitted on the whole dataset. The R frame name only names the data frame variable. Input frames name the step the rows come from, here sv-convert_booleans_to_numbers. Variable substitution resolves PDI variables in the script text; it does not change how many rows arrive.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The prediction step was copied from the training step and its R frame name left as train, while its script reads as.data.frame(test).
questions.prompt: What happens when it runs?
options: It scores the training rows instead of the new ones
The script fails, as the rows arrive in R as train
It works, as PDI renames the frame to suit the script
It works, as R frame name is only a display label
questions.explanation: The R frame name is the name of the data frame variable the incoming rows appear as in R, so with train set there is no test object for the script to read. It is not a display label. The rows are the prediction step's own input, only under the wrong name. PDI does not rewrite the script or rename the frame to match it.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: A new team member asks how the pieces of the fraud solution fit together, from raw data to flagged transactions.
questions.prompt: Which order is right?
options: Score transactions, train GBM on the scores, then run AutoML
Prepare data, shortlist with AutoML, train GBM in R, then score
Run AutoML in PDI, then send each transaction to Colab
Train GBM in R, run AutoML on it, then prepare the data
questions.explanation: PDI prepares the data and writes H2O.csv, AutoML in Colab shortlists models and points to GBM, PDI trains a GBM in R and saves gbm_fraud.rdata, and a separate transformation loads it to score new transactions. Scoring needs a trained model first. AutoML needs the prepared data before any model exists. AutoML runs in Colab, and scoring runs in PDI.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The whole solution folder is copied to another machine under a different path. Training and prediction still find gbm_fraud.rdata without any edits.
questions.prompt: Why does the handoff survive the move?
options: Both paths start from the transformation's folder
R remembers the last file it saved and reloads it
PDI searches the whole disk for the .rdata file
The model is stored inside the job file itself
questions.explanation: Both scripts use ${Internal.Transformation.Filename.Directory}/train_model_output/gbm_fraud.rdata, so the path follows wherever the transformations sit. PDI does not search for files. The job references the transformations; it does not hold the model. Each R session starts fresh and remembers nothing.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: The training transformation is renamed and moved into a subfolder for tidiness. The job that runs it is not edited, and its next run fails.
questions.prompt: Why does the run fail?
options: The job refers to the file's old location, not a copy of it
A rename is harmless, but moving the file breaks the job
The job holds a stale copy of the transformation inside it
The job compiles each .ktr into itself when it is saved
questions.explanation: A job entry points at its transformation, which is why Spoon offers Open referenced object, so renaming or moving the file breaks the reference until the entry is updated. The job embeds no copy. A rename alone also breaks it, since the reference names the file. Nothing is compiled in, which is also why an edited transformation needs no rebuild of the job.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card

questions.scenario: A reviewer who does not use PDI needs to look through last night's scored transactions and their fraud probabilities.
questions.prompt: What does the prediction workflow give them?
options: An entry for each transaction in kettle.properties
gbm_fraud.rdata, which also stores each prediction
H2O.csv, refreshed with each night's new scores
credit_card_predict.xlsx, in train_model_output
questions.explanation: The results are written to credit_card_predict.xlsx in the train_model_output folder, a file a reviewer can open and sort, and which can also trigger further events downstream. The .rdata file holds the model and best_trees, not predictions. H2O.csv is the AutoML upload. kettle.properties holds PDI variables, not results.
questions.source: Pentaho Developer - ML Specialty: Credit Card
